title: Folio from a Qur'an Manuscript

image.credit: The Metropolitan Museum of Art, Gift of Rudolf M. Riefstahl, 1930
image.license: Public domain. Released under Creative Commons Zero (CC0) through the Met's Open Access program

altText: A wide, rectangular parchment page with seven lines of bold black Arabic script. The letters are stretched out horizontally, and small colored dots appear among them.

source.verifiedBy: Met Collection API object record: title, date, medium, country, credit line, public-domain flag, classification, tag (Qur'an) and image URLs read from the record; museum page text read for the script, number of lines, ink, and dots

context: A page from a Qur'an made in the late 9th or early 10th century, probably in Syria, with seven lines written in early kufic script in black ink on parchment. The Met notes that red and green dots mark the vowels.

descriptions.k: This page has seven lines of big, bold writing. It is from the Qur'an, a holy book for Muslims. The writing is black and the letters are stretched out wide. Little red and green dots sit among them. Can you find a dot?
descriptions.g12: This page is from a very old Qur'an, the holy book of Islam. It was written by hand more than a thousand years ago on parchment, which is animal skin. There are seven lines of wide, bold letters. Tiny red and green dots help readers. Why do you think the letters are stretched so wide?
descriptions.g35: This is a page from a Qur'an, written by hand on parchment in the late 800s or early 900s, probably in Syria. The page is wider than it is tall, and the letters are stretched out horizontally to fit it. A broad reed pen made the black strokes, and red and green dots mark vowels. Look at the seven lines and the spaces between them. Why might the writer have chosen a wide page and wide letters?
descriptions.g68: Early Qur'an manuscripts like this one were written in an angular style called early kufic, on parchment, the prepared skin of an animal. The Met notes seven lines of text in horizontally elongated letters that suit the rectangular page, softened by rounded letters whose inner spaces are tiny. A broad-nibbed reed pen made the black strokes, and red and green dots mark vowels. How does the shape of the page influence the shape of the letters?
descriptions.g910: This folio from a dispersed Qur'an, probably made in Syria in the late 9th or early 10th century, exemplifies early kufic. The Met describes horizontally elongated letters that echo the page's rectangular format, with angular forms softened by rounded letters that look like large black dots. Ink was applied with a broad-nibbed reed pen on the good side of the parchment, and red and green dots mark vowels. Consider how page shape, script, and spacing create rhythm in a text that was meant for reverent reading.
descriptions.g1112: Before the later cursive hands became standard for the Qur'an, early kufic manuscripts like this one used elongated, angular letters on horizontal parchment pages. The Met connects the stretched letterforms to the rectangular format and describes rounded letters whose counters shrink almost to points. Colored dots mark vowels, showing how the written text supported correct recitation. As a folio from a dispersed manuscript, known as the Riefstahl Qur'an fragment, it raises questions about reconstructing a book from its scattered parts and about how sacred text is displayed in museums.

safety.method: Title, medium, classification (Codices) and tag (Qur'an) checked against the museum record, and the museum page text read: calligraphy only, no figural imagery. The image file itself was not visually inspected in this build. A person should confirm it in the review tool before release. Religious content to be presented respectfully and factually; the text is described as writing and not translated.

teacherNote.context: An early kufic Qur'an page on parchment, probably made in Syria around 900. It is part of a dispersed manuscript sometimes called the Riefstahl Qur'an fragment.
directions: Have students write a short phrase with a chisel-tip marker, stretching the letters horizontally, and compare with normal handwriting.
Discuss how a broken-up manuscript might be reconstructed and what is lost when pages are separated.
Compare with the other Qur'an folio in the archive, noting the differences in script, material, and decoration.
